title: The Memory Taxonomy: working, episodic, semantic, procedural
summary: An agent has no memory of its own — the model is stateless, so every kind of 'remembering' is something you engineer. Borrowing from cognitive science, we split agent memory into four types: working (what's in the context window right now), episodic (records of past interactions), semantic (durable facts the agent knows), and procedural (how the agent does things). Knowing which type you need tells you where a piece of information should live.

subtopics.title: The model is stateless; memory is engineered
subtopics.explanation: An LLM call has no recollection of any previous call — you get exactly the input you send and nothing more. Every 'memory' an agent appears to have is data you deliberately put back into the next prompt. This is the foundational fact behind the whole taxonomy: each memory type is just a different strategy for deciding what to re-supply.
subtopics.example:
# each call is independent - the model remembers nothing on its own
reply1 = llm([{"role": "user", "content": "My name is Ada."}])
reply2 = llm([{"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"}])
# reply2 has NO idea - the name was never re-sent
# 'memory' only exists if YOU carry it forward:
history = [{"role": "user", "content": "My name is Ada."}]
history.append({"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"})
reply = llm(history)   # now it can answer 'Ada'

subtopics.title: Working memory is the context window
subtopics.explanation: Working memory is whatever currently sits inside the context window: the system prompt, the running message list, tool results, and retrieved snippets. It is fast, immediate, and volatile — when the request ends, it is gone unless persisted. Recognizing that working memory is just the window makes it clear why it is finite and must be budgeted, the theme every later topic returns to.
subtopics.example:
# working memory = the full prompt assembled for THIS call
working_memory = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},   # instructions
    {"role": "user", "content": "Book a table for tonight."},
    {"role": "tool", "content": "7pm slot available"},   # observation
]
# everything the model 'knows' right now lives in this list
reply = llm(working_memory)
# after the response returns, nothing here survives automatically

subtopics.title: Episodic memory: records of past interactions
subtopics.explanation: Episodic memory stores specific past events — earlier conversations, prior tool calls, what happened on a given date — so the agent can recall 'that time we did X'. It is typically kept outside the window in a log or vector store and pulled back in when relevant. Episodic memory is what lets an agent reference a conversation from last week even though that week's tokens left the window long ago.
subtopics.example:
# an episode = one recorded interaction, saved for later recall
episode = {
    "timestamp": "2026-07-01T14:30",
    "user": "Reschedule my Tuesday demo to Thursday.",
    "outcome": "moved demo 2026-07-02 -> 2026-07-04",
}
episodic_store.append(episode)   # lives outside the window
# later, when the user says 'undo that reschedule', you fetch it back
relevant = episodic_store.search("demo reschedule")

subtopics.title: Semantic memory: durable facts the agent knows
subtopics.explanation: Semantic memory holds general, timeless knowledge and stable facts: the user's name, their preferences, company policies, product details. Unlike an episode, it is not tied to a moment — it is the distilled 'what is true'. Semantic memory is how an agent carries a user's standing preferences across sessions without re-reading every past conversation.
subtopics.example:
# semantic memory = stable facts, not tied to any single event
user_profile = {
    "name": "Ada",
    "timezone": "Europe/London",
    "prefers": "concise answers, metric units",
    "dietary": "vegetarian",
}
# inject the relevant facts into the window when they matter
system = SYSTEM_PROMPT + f"\nUser facts: {user_profile}"
reply = llm([{"role": "system", "content": system}, latest_msg])

subtopics.title: Procedural memory: learned how-to
subtopics.explanation: Procedural memory encodes how the agent performs tasks — the workflows, tool-use patterns, and rules baked into its system prompt, few-shot examples, or fine-tuned weights. It is the 'skill', not the 'fact'. Procedural memory is what makes an agent reliably follow your preferred process step after step without being re-taught each turn.
subtopics.example:
# procedural memory = the HOW, usually in the system prompt / examples
PROCEDURE = '''When refunding an order:
1. verify the order exists with get_order
2. check it is within the 30-day window
3. call issue_refund, then confirm to the user
'''
system = {"role": "system", "content": PROCEDURE}
# the agent follows this workflow every time, without relearning it
reply = llm([system, {"role": "user", "content": "Refund order A-12."}])

foundations.overview: Because an LLM is stateless between calls, an agent's 'memory' is entirely a systems-engineering choice: what you re-supply, and from where. A useful map, borrowed from human cognition, splits it into four types. Working memory is the context window — the immediate, volatile scratchpad holding the current prompt. Episodic memory records specific past events (conversations, actions) so they can be recalled later. Semantic memory holds durable, timeless facts like preferences and policies. Procedural memory is the learned how-to — workflows and patterns encoded in prompts, examples, or weights. The human analogy is useful precisely because it forces the right question for any piece of information: is this a momentary detail (working), a specific thing that happened (episodic), a lasting truth (semantic), or a way of doing things (procedural)? That question tells you where the data should live and how it should re-enter the window.
foundations.formalDefinition: Agent memory is the set of mechanisms by which information persists across otherwise-stateless model calls. It is conventionally decomposed into working memory (the current context window), episodic memory (stored records of specific past interactions), semantic memory (durable general facts and knowledge), and procedural memory (encoded skills, workflows, and behavioural patterns).
foundations.whyItMatters: Every serious agent problem — losing track of a conversation, forgetting a user's preference, repeating a mistake, running out of context — is a memory problem in disguise. Naming the four types gives you a vocabulary to diagnose which memory is missing or overflowing and to choose the right fix, instead of dumping everything into one ever-growing prompt.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the agent as an employee with a whiteboard, a diary, a rolodex, and a training manual. The whiteboard (working memory) holds what they're doing right now and gets wiped often; the diary (episodic) logs what happened on which day; the rolodex (semantic) stores facts they can always look up; and the training manual (procedural) tells them how the job is done. You decide what gets written where — and what gets copied back onto the whiteboard when it's needed.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A support agent uses semantic memory for a customer's plan and preferences, episodic memory to recall last week's ticket, procedural memory for the refund workflow, and working memory for the live chat turn. A coding assistant keeps project conventions as semantic memory, past edits as episodic, its edit-test loop as procedural, and the open files as working memory.
commonUseCases: Deciding whether a fact belongs in the prompt, a store, or the system message
Diagnosing 'the agent forgot X' by asking which memory type failed
Recalling specific past interactions on demand (episodic)

commonMisconceptions.myth: The model remembers previous messages on its own.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The model is stateless — it only sees what you send this call. Any continuity is you carrying prior content forward into the next prompt.

commonMisconceptions.myth: All memory is just 'the conversation history'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: History is only working/episodic content in the window. Durable facts (semantic) and workflows (procedural) are distinct types that usually live outside the running message list.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More memory in the prompt is always better.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The window is finite and costly, and irrelevant memory hurts focus. Good memory design is about supplying the right type at the right moment, not maximising volume.

interactiveWidget.title: The four memories, one agent
interactiveWidget.caption: A single mental picture that keeps working, episodic, semantic, and procedural memory straight.

config.note: Picture the agent as a new hire on their first shift. In front of them is a whiteboard covered in the current task — the caller's name, the slot they just checked, the note a tool handed back. That's working memory: vivid, immediate, and wiped clean the moment the shift ends. In a drawer sits a dated diary — 'Tuesday: moved Ada's demo to Thursday' — the episodic record of things that actually happened, thumbed through only when something jogs it loose. On the desk is a rolodex of standing truths: Ada is vegetarian, she likes metric units, she's in London. Those facts don't belong to any one day; that's semantic memory. And pinned to the wall is the laminated procedure — 'to refund: verify, check the window, issue, confirm' — the how-to the hire follows every single time. Nothing moves between these on its own. The whole craft of agent memory is deciding, turn by turn, which scraps get copied from the drawer, the rolodex, and the wall back onto that small, crowded whiteboard.

checkpoints.prompt: A user tells your agent 'I'm vegetarian' and expects it to remember this next month. Which memory type should store that fact?
checkpoints.explanation: A standing, timeless truth about the user ('is vegetarian') is a durable fact — semantic memory. It isn't tied to a single event (episodic) and shouldn't live only in the volatile window (working).

checkpoints.prompt: Given the model is stateless, what does the second call print?
checkpoints.code:
reply1 = llm([{"role": "user", "content": "Remember the code is 4821."}])
reply2 = llm([{"role": "user", "content": "What was the code?"}])
print(reply2)  # the second call sees ONLY its own message
options: The model cannot know the code; it was never re-sent
checkpoints.explanation: Each call is independent. The second call's input contains only 'What was the code?' — the model never received '4821', so it cannot recall it. Continuity requires you to carry prior content forward.

checkpoints.prompt: An agent reliably follows your refund workflow (verify, check window, issue, confirm) every session. Where does that behaviour live?
options: Procedural memory (e.g. the system prompt / examples)
The vector store of past chats
checkpoints.explanation: A learned how-to — a workflow the agent applies every time — is procedural memory, typically encoded in the system prompt, few-shot examples, or fine-tuned weights. It's the 'skill', not a fact or a specific past event.

keyTakeaways: The model is stateless; every kind of agent memory is information you deliberately re-supply to the next call.
Working memory is the context window — immediate, volatile, finite, and must be budgeted.
Episodic memory records specific past interactions and lives outside the window until recalled.
Semantic memory holds durable, timeless facts (preferences, policies); procedural memory holds learned how-to (workflows, patterns).
Naming the four types turns vague 'the agent forgot' problems into a precise question: which memory was missing or overflowing?
